tips.title: Two ureters, one urethra
tips.body: A **ureter** runs from each kidney to the bladder, so there are **two**. The **urethra** carries urine out of the body, and there is **one**. Getting them the wrong way round is avoidable and common.

tips.title: The liver makes urea, the kidney removes it
tips.body: Excess **amino acids** cannot be stored, so the **liver** breaks them down into **urea**. The blood carries it to the **kidney**, which filters it out. Saying the kidney makes urea is a clear error.

tips.title: Too large to be filtered
tips.body: **Proteins and blood cells** stay in the blood because filtration works by **size**. That one phrase — *too large to be filtered* — answers a whole family of questions about what is and is not in the filtrate.

tips.title: Follow the ADH chain in order
tips.body: **ADH → permeability of the collecting duct → water reabsorbed → volume and concentration of urine.** Questions give you one end and ask for the other, so learn it as a chain and you can start from either.

tips.title: No urea, same glucose
tips.body: Dialysis fluid has **no urea**, so urea diffuses out down a steep gradient; and the **same glucose** as blood, so there is no gradient and none is lost. The fluid's composition is what does the work.

why.matters:
Cells sit in a watery solution and water crosses their membranes by **osmosis**, so the concentration of the blood is not a detail — too dilute and cells burst, too concentrated and they shrink. Something has to hold it steady whatever you drink.

The kidneys do that and dispose of **urea** at the same time. Their method is surprising: throw nearly everything out of the blood, then take back exactly what is wanted. It sounds wasteful and it is the reason the system works at all.

examples.title: Why the kidney throws out the glucose and then takes it back
examples.body:
Filtration in the kidney works by **size**. Small molecules are pushed out of the blood and large ones — proteins, blood cells — stay behind, and that is the only distinction it can make.

So glucose leaves too, along with the water, ions and urea. Sorting happens afterwards, in **reabsorption**: all the glucose is taken back, and as much water as the body needs. It is the same logic as tipping out a drawer to find one thing — crude, and far simpler than a filter that could recognise every molecule it met.

examples.title: Why your urine is darker in the morning
examples.body:
You have gone eight hours without drinking, so the blood is a little concentrated. The pituitary responds by releasing more **ADH**, which makes the **collecting duct** more permeable to water.

More water is therefore reabsorbed into the blood, and what is left is a small volume of concentrated, dark urine. Drink a litre of water and the opposite happens within the hour: less ADH, a less permeable duct, and a large volume of pale urine. The colour is a readout of a feedback loop.

examples.title: What is in a bag of dialysis fluid, and why
examples.body:
Dialysis works entirely by **diffusion**, so every ingredient of the fluid is a decision about a concentration gradient.

It contains **no urea**, so urea diffuses out of the blood down a steep gradient and keeps going. It contains the **same glucose** as blood, so there is no gradient and none is lost. And it has the ion concentration of **healthy** blood, so a patient with too much of an ion loses the excess and stops there. Nothing is pumped: the recipe does the sorting.

steps.title: Why water content must be controlled
steps.body:
Cells sit in a watery solution, and water moves in and out of them by **osmosis** — from where it is more dilute to where it is more concentrated, through the partially permeable cell membrane.

That makes the concentration of the blood a matter of life and death for a cell:

- If the blood becomes **too dilute**, water moves **into** the cells. An animal cell has no cell wall, so it **swells and may burst**.
- If the blood becomes **too concentrated**, water moves **out** of the cells. They **shrink**, and the reactions inside them cannot work properly.

Keeping the water content of the blood constant is called **osmoregulation**, and it is done by the **kidneys**.

Water is gained by **drinking** and from **food**, and lost in **urine**, in **sweat**, in **breath** and in faeces. Of those, only the amount lost in **urine** can be adjusted — you cannot choose to sweat less on a hot day. So the kidney is the organ that makes the balance work.

One piece of vocabulary worth getting right: a **plant** cell has a **cell wall**, so it does not burst; it becomes turgid. This topic is about **animal** cells, which do.

steps.title: The urinary system
steps.body:
The **urinary system** has four parts, and the specification asks you to describe its structure.

- **Kidneys** — two of them. They **filter the blood** and make urine.
- **Ureters** — two tubes, one from each kidney, carrying urine to the bladder.
- **Bladder** — stores urine.
- **Urethra** — the single tube carrying urine out of the body.

Blood arrives at each kidney through the **renal artery** and leaves through the **renal vein**. *Renal* simply means *of the kidney*.

Two names are easy to swap, and the difference is worth fixing now: a **ureter** carries urine **from a kidney to the bladder**, and there are **two**; the **urethra** carries it **out of the body**, and there is **one**.

**Where the urea comes from.** The body cannot store excess **amino acids**. In the **liver**, the excess is broken down, and this produces **urea** — a toxic waste product which is carried in the blood to the kidneys and removed. So the liver makes urea and the kidney removes it, which is a distinction questions test directly.

steps.title: ADH and the collecting duct
steps.body:
The amount of **water** reabsorbed is adjusted by a hormone: **ADH**, antidiuretic hormone, released by the **pituitary gland**.

ADH acts on the **collecting duct** of the nephron, and what it changes is the duct's **permeability to water**:

**If the blood is too concentrated** (you have sweated, or not drunk enough):

- **more ADH** is released
- the collecting duct becomes **more permeable** to water
- **more water is reabsorbed** into the blood
- the result is a **small volume of concentrated urine**

**If the blood is too dilute** (you have drunk a lot):

- **less ADH** is released
- the collecting duct becomes **less permeable**
- **less water is reabsorbed**
- the result is a **large volume of dilute urine**

The chain is always the same four links: **ADH → permeability → water reabsorbed → volume and concentration of urine**. Questions give you one end and ask for the other, so learning it as a chain rather than as two lists means you can start from either end.

And this is **negative feedback** once more: the response opposes the change. Blood too concentrated leads to water being kept, which dilutes it back.

steps.title: When the kidneys fail
steps.body:
If the kidneys stop working, **urea and excess water and ions build up** in the blood. Urea is toxic, and the change in water and ion balance damages cells. Kidney failure is fatal if untreated. There are two treatments.

**Kidney dialysis.** A machine does the kidney's job. Blood is taken from the body and flows on one side of a **partially permeable membrane**; **dialysis fluid** flows on the other.

The dialysis fluid is made to contain:

- the **same concentration of glucose and ions** as healthy blood, so **none of those is lost** — there is no concentration difference for them to diffuse down
- **no urea**, so urea **diffuses out** of the blood down a steep concentration gradient

That design is the clever part, and it is regularly examined: the fluid's composition decides what is removed and what is kept.

Dialysis must be repeated regularly — typically several sessions a week, each of several hours — and the diet must be controlled between sessions.

**A kidney transplant.** A kidney from a donor is placed in the body. It works continuously, so there is no need for regular treatment and no dietary restriction.

But the recipient's **immune system may reject** the donor kidney as foreign, so **immunosuppressant drugs** must be taken, which leave the patient more vulnerable to infection. And donor kidneys are **in short supply**, so there is a waiting list.

steps.title: Going deeper: why filter first and take it back?
steps.body:
**The obvious question.** Filtering out glucose and then reabsorbing all of it looks wasteful. Why not leave it in the blood to begin with?

Because **filtration cannot select**. It works by **size**: blood is pushed at high pressure through a membrane, and anything small enough goes through. Urea is small, so it passes — but so do water, glucose and ions, because they are small too. There is no way to filter out urea alone.

So the kidney uses a two-stage design: **filter indiscriminately by size, then take back selectively what is useful.** That is exactly what **selective reabsorption** means, and the word *selective* is the contrast with the unselective filtration before it.

This also explains **why glucose in the urine is a sign of diabetes**. Normally all the filtered glucose is reabsorbed. If the blood glucose concentration is very high, more glucose is filtered than the nephron can take back, and the excess appears in the urine. The kidney has not failed; it has been overwhelmed.

**Evaluating the two treatments.** A question asking you to compare dialysis and transplant wants both sides and a judgement:

- **Dialysis** is available to everyone who needs it and carries no rejection risk, but it is **time consuming**, restricts the **diet**, and must continue indefinitely.
- **A transplant** restores normal life and needs no regular treatment, but donor kidneys are **scarce**, surgery carries risk, the kidney **may be rejected**, and **immunosuppressants** leave the patient vulnerable to infection.

A sensible judgement: a transplant is generally better **when a matching kidney is available**, and dialysis is what keeps a patient alive **until** one is — which is closer to how the two are actually used than declaring either superior.

**Three points of precision.**

- **Two ureters, one urethra.** Swapping them is common and avoidable.
- **The liver makes urea; the kidney removes it.** Saying the kidney makes urea is a clear error.
- **ADH changes permeability**, not the amount of filtering. The kidney filters the same volume; what changes is how much water is **taken back**.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Water moves in and out of cells by **osmosis**. Blood **too dilute** makes an animal cell **burst**; **too concentrated** makes it **shrink**.
- **Osmoregulation** is control of the water content of the blood, done by the **kidneys**.
- The urinary system: **kidneys → ureters → bladder → urethra**. Two ureters, one urethra.
- **Urea** is made in the **liver**, from the breakdown of **excess amino acids**, and removed by the kidneys.
- Each kidney contains about a million **nephrons**.
- **Filtration**: blood at high pressure in the **glomerulus** and **Bowman's capsule**. **Water, glucose, ions and urea** are filtered out.
- **Proteins and blood cells are too large** to be filtered.
- **Selective reabsorption**: **all the glucose** is taken back, because it is useful.
- **Water reabsorption** is adjusted according to need; what is left becomes **urine**.
- **ADH** from the **pituitary** changes the **permeability of the collecting duct** to water.
- Blood **too concentrated** → **more ADH** → more permeable → **more water reabsorbed** → a **small volume of concentrated urine**.
- Blood **too dilute** → **less ADH** → less water reabsorbed → a **large volume of dilute urine**.
- **Dialysis**: the fluid has **no urea** so urea diffuses out, and the **same glucose** as blood so none is lost.
- **Transplant**: no regular treatment, but donors are scarce and the kidney may be **rejected**.

questions.prompt: Describe how a nephron filters the blood and forms urine, naming the structures involved and explaining what happens to glucose, water and urea.
questions.solution: Blood arrives at the nephron under high pressure in a knot of capillaries called the glomerulus, which sits inside a structure called the Bowman's capsule. The high pressure forces small molecules out of the blood and into the capsule. These include water, glucose, ions and urea. Proteins and blood cells are not filtered out because they are too large to pass through, so they remain in the blood. The liquid that has been filtered then passes along the nephron, where selective reabsorption takes place. All of the glucose is reabsorbed back into the blood, because glucose is useful to the body and none should be wasted. Some of the water is also reabsorbed, and the amount depends on how much water the body needs at the time. Urea is not reabsorbed, because it is a toxic waste product that must be removed. What remains at the end, which is the urea together with the excess water and excess ions, passes out of the nephron as urine.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Filtration.** Blood arrives at **high pressure** in the **glomerulus**, a knot of capillaries inside the **Bowman's capsule**. The pressure forces **small molecules** out into the capsule: **water, glucose, ions and urea**.

**Proteins and blood cells** are **too large** to be filtered, so they stay in the blood. That is what makes it filtration — it separates by **size**.

**Selective reabsorption.**

- **All the glucose** is reabsorbed into the blood, because it is useful and none should be wasted.
- **Some water** is reabsorbed, and how much depends on what the body needs.
- **Urea is not reabsorbed** — it is toxic waste that must be removed.

**What is left.** Urea, together with the excess water and excess ions, passes on as **urine**.

The word **selective** is the contrast with the filtration before it: filtering cannot choose, so the nephron filters everything small and then takes back what it wants.

questions.prompt: Compare kidney dialysis with a kidney transplant as treatments for kidney failure, and explain how the composition of dialysis fluid allows it to clean the blood.
questions.solution: In kidney dialysis, blood from the patient is passed through a machine where it flows on one side of a partially permeable membrane, with dialysis fluid flowing on the other side. The dialysis fluid contains no urea at all, so there is a steep concentration gradient and urea diffuses out of the blood and into the fluid. The fluid contains the same concentration of glucose as normal blood, so there is no concentration gradient for glucose and none of it is lost from the blood. It also contains ions at the concentration found in healthy blood, so that any excess ions are removed while normal levels are maintained. Dialysis is available to everyone who needs it and there is no risk of rejection, but it must be repeated several times a week for several hours at a time, and the patient's diet has to be controlled between sessions. A kidney transplant gives the patient a donor kidney which works continuously, so no regular treatment is needed and the diet can be normal. However, donor kidneys are in short supply, the surgery carries risks, and the patient's immune system may reject the donated kidney, so immunosuppressant drugs must be taken, which leave the patient more vulnerable to infection. On balance a transplant is generally preferable when a suitable kidney is available, while dialysis keeps a patient alive until one can be found.

questions.modelAnswer:
**How dialysis works.** Blood flows on one side of a **partially permeable membrane**; **dialysis fluid** flows on the other. What the fluid contains decides what is removed:

- **No urea** → a steep **concentration gradient**, so urea **diffuses out** of the blood.
- **The same glucose concentration as blood** → **no gradient**, so **no glucose is lost**.
- **Ions at healthy blood levels** → excess ions are removed while normal levels are kept.

**Dialysis.**

- *For:* available to everyone who needs it; no rejection risk.
- *Against:* several sessions a week of several hours each; the diet must be controlled; it continues indefinitely.

**Transplant.**

- *For:* the kidney works continuously, so normal life and a normal diet.
- *Against:* donor kidneys are **scarce**; surgery carries risk; the kidney may be **rejected**, so **immunosuppressants** are needed, raising the risk of infection.

**Judgement.** A transplant is generally preferable **when a suitable kidney is available**; dialysis is what keeps a patient alive **until** one is found. That is closer to how the two are actually used than declaring either simply better.

examTechnique.body:
Name the structures: glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, collecting duct. A description that says the kidney filters the blood without naming where loses marks.

Say that proteins and blood cells are too large to be filtered, rather than that they are not filtered.

For glucose, say that all of it is reabsorbed and that this is selective reabsorption.

For ADH, work through the chain in order and include the permeability step, which is the one most often skipped.

For dialysis, explain the composition of the fluid in terms of concentration gradients rather than describing the machine.

When comparing dialysis with a transplant, give both sides and finish with a judgement.
examinerErrors: Saying the kidney produces urea rather than removing it.
Swapping the ureter and the urethra.
Saying proteins are reabsorbed rather than never filtered.
Saying some glucose is reabsorbed, when all of it is.
Saying ADH changes how much blood is filtered rather than the permeability of the collecting duct.
Getting the ADH direction backwards: more ADH gives concentrated urine, not dilute.
Explaining dialysis without mentioning concentration gradients.
Saying a transplant has no disadvantages.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer explains the two-stage design rather than reciting it: filtration cannot select because it works by size, so the nephron filters everything small and then takes back what is useful. That single insight explains selective reabsorption, why glucose appears in the urine in untreated diabetes, and why dialysis fluid must be made up so carefully. It follows the ADH chain through the permeability step every time. And in the evaluation it notices that dialysis and transplant are not really rivals — one sustains a patient until the other becomes possible.
